# It Would Have Been Enough to Say Sorry

[Silas Bambil · March 2025]{.meta}

A friend once wronged me, and what I had initially considered a straightforward matter became something much more troubling. I had expected that we could discuss what had happened, acknowledge where things had gone wrong, and move on. Instead, I found myself having to explain why I had any reason to be upset in the first place. The conversation gradually became less about what my friend had done and more about how I had interpreted it. I had approached someone I cared about, hoping for a little understanding, and somehow found myself having to defend the legitimacy of my own feelings.

I have come to regard a persistent inability to take accountability as one of the most dangerous qualities a person can possess. I am not particularly troubled by the fact that people make mistakes. I have made enough of my own to appreciate how easily one can exercise poor judgement, behave inconsiderately, or hurt someone without intending to. What concerns me is how people respond when their mistakes are brought to their attention. A person's behaviour in that moment can reveal far more about them than the original wrongdoing. It is often that response, rather than the mistake itself, that makes me reconsider how I regard someone.

There is something remarkable about the amount of effort some people will invest in avoiding two words: I'm sorry. They will explain the circumstances, justify their intentions, question your interpretation, and somehow find a way to present themselves as the injured party. By the time the conversation ends, you may have discussed practically everything except the very thing that prompted it. I was not asking my friend to write a dissertation explaining what had happened. I had hoped that someone who knew me well enough to be my friend would also care enough to acknowledge that something they had done had hurt me.

In a sense, I felt that I had been wronged twice. There was the original disappointment, and then there was the experience of being made to feel unreasonable for expressing it. I found myself questioning whether I was being unnecessarily sensitive and whether I should have raised the matter at all. It was frustrating to discover that my reaction had become more objectionable than the behaviour that had prompted it. Sometimes, what ultimately damages a friendship is not the mistake itself but everything somebody does afterwards to avoid admitting that it was a mistake.

Disrespect does not always announce itself. Sometimes, it appears in the form of a joke or a seemingly harmless remark whose implications become more apparent upon reflection. I do not believe that every insensitive joke is an expression of malice. People make unfortunate jokes, and intentions deserve consideration. However, I find it unreasonable to be expected to appreciate somebody's intentions when they are unwilling to give comparable consideration to my experience. Surely, discovering that something I found amusing had hurt a friend would give me reason to reconsider it. An explanation of why you stepped on my foot does not make it unreasonable for me to tell you that it hurts.

I am perfectly capable of questioning my own interpretation of events. I can misunderstand people, become unnecessarily offended, or attach significance to something that was never intended to carry it. I would like to think that I possess enough intellectual humility to reconsider my position when given a good reason to do so. However, being willing to question myself does not mean I must indefinitely entertain explanations that dismiss my concerns. I can acknowledge the possibility that I am wrong without accepting that I must always be wrong whenever somebody finds taking responsibility inconvenient.

I must also be willing to hold myself to the same standard. I have behaved poorly, disappointed people, and handled situations in ways I subsequently regretted. Sometimes, the circumstances surrounding my behaviour might help someone understand why I acted as I did. That does not necessarily make my behaviour acceptable. I would find it hypocritical to expect accountability from others while regarding my own circumstances as sufficient justification whenever I disappoint somebody. If I have hurt someone I care about, I want to be capable of explaining myself without making that explanation a substitute for an apology.

My concern extends beyond the immediate disagreement. If someone cannot acknowledge that their behaviour was inappropriate, what reassurance do I have that things will be different when similar circumstances arise? I do not want to maintain a friendship in which expressing disappointment regularly requires me to prepare a defence of my own character. Sometimes, the exhaustion of a disagreement has very little to do with the seriousness of the original offence. It comes from the effort of trying to resolve something that should not have been so difficult. Eventually, even the thought of raising another concern becomes tiring.

I have never expected friendships to exist without disagreements. Friends will misunderstand one another, exercise poor judgement, and occasionally say things they subsequently regret. What gives me confidence in a friendship is knowing that we can discuss these things honestly. I want to be able to tell a friend that something they did bothered me, just as I want them to feel comfortable telling me when I have behaved poorly. The affection I have for someone should make me more receptive to their concerns, not less. I do not require people to be incapable of hurting me. I require that we be capable of talking about it when they do.

I find it unfortunate that some people appear to regard admitting a mistake as a greater loss than damaging a meaningful relationship. I had no interest in humiliating my friend, extracting a confession, or enjoying the satisfaction of being proven right. What would I have gained from winning an argument if, in the process, I lost some of the affection and confidence I had previously associated with our friendship? I simply wanted an acknowledgement. An apology would not have diminished my regard for my friend. If anything, the willingness to offer one would have given me another reason to value our relationship.

I have learnt that there is only so much I can do in such circumstances. I can explain how I felt, listen to another person's perspective, reconsider my interpretation, and acknowledge my own shortcomings. I cannot compel somebody to offer a sincere apology, nor do I want to spend an unreasonable amount of time trying to obtain one. When someone consistently refuses to take responsibility for their behaviour, I can reconsider how much trust and emotional energy I invest in that relationship. I do not have to resent somebody or disregard everything I once appreciated about them to recognise that I might need to regard them differently.

What remains disappointing about the experience that prompted this reflection is how little I had initially wanted from my friend. I was not expecting perfection or asking for an extraordinary demonstration of remorse. I simply wanted someone I cared about to acknowledge that something they had done had hurt me. Instead, I found myself reconsidering things about our friendship that I had previously had little reason to question. It is rather unfortunate how much one can discover about a relationship while asking for something so simple. It would have been enough to say sorry.
